entities.evidence: The verse names Eve as the man's wife and identifies her as Cain's mother.
Cain is the name of the son Eve bears in this verse.
Eve explicitly names Yahweh, the same God who brought the woman to the man in Genesis 2:22.

review.translation: [Then the man|0] [lay with|1] [Eve|3,2], [his wife|4], [and she conceived|5] [and bore|6] [Cain|8,7]. [And she said|9], “[I have gained|10] [a man|11] [with|12] {the help of} [Yahweh|13]!”

analysis.evidence: The article marks אָדָם as definite. He is the subject of יָדַע, and the phrase חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ identifies Eve as his wife, fixing the reference to the first man.
analysis.morphology: Conjunction וְ plus definite article הָ plus masculine singular absolute noun אָדָם.

analysis.evidence: The direct object אֶת חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ identifies Eve, his wife. The next words, וַתַּהַר וַתֵּלֶד אֶת קַיִן, say that she conceived and bore Cain, establishing the sexual sense of יָדַע here.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, third person masculine singular, with no prefix or suffix
analysis.sense: to have sexual intercourse with someone

analysis.evidence: In יָדַע אֶת חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ, אֶת marks the proper name חַוָּה as the definite direct object of יָדַע, “knew.” The appositive אִשְׁתּוֹ, “his wife,” further identifies Eve.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew direct-object particle without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: אֶת marks חַוָּה as the direct object of יָדַע. The following אִשְׁתּוֹ, “his wife,” stands in apposition and identifies Eve as the man's wife.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular proper noun, without prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Personal name given to the man's wife.

analysis.evidence: In אֶת חַוָּה אִשְׁתּוֹ, the noun stands in apposition to Eve’s name. The suffix ־וֹ refers to הָאָדָם, identifying Eve as his wife.
analysis.morphology: Feminine singular common noun in construct with a third-person masculine singular possessive suffix.

analysis.evidence: Eve is the subject of the paired verbs וַתַּהַר וַתֵּלֶד. After the man knew her, she conceived and then gave birth to Cain.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third-person feminine singular, with prefixed וַ־

analysis.evidence: Eve is the subject of both וַתַּהַר “she conceived” and וַתֵּלֶד. The direct object אֶת קַיִן identifies Cain as the child she bore.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person feminine singular, with prefixed וַ־.

analysis.evidence: In וַתֵּלֶד אֶת קַיִן, “she bore Cain,” אֶת marks the proper name קַיִן as the definite direct object of וַתֵּלֶד.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew direct-object particle in the short form אֶת, without prefix or suffix.

draft.change: Add a personal-name article for Cain with its etymology left open pending evidence.
draft.definition: Cain, the son born to Adam and Eve in Genesis 4:1.
draft.evidence: Genesis 4:1 identifies the child by name in וַתֵּלֶד אֶת קַיִן and immediately gives Eve's words קָנִיתִי אִישׁ.

analysis.evidence: וַתֵּלֶד אֶת קַיִן means “she bore Cain.” Eve then says קָנִיתִי אִישׁ, “I have acquired a man.” Her words echo the sound of the child's name, but the wordplay alone does not establish its derivation.
analysis.morphology: Masculine singular personal name, without prefix or suffix. The separate אֶת marks it as the direct object of וַתֵּלֶד.
analysis.sense: The personal name of the son Eve bears to Adam in Genesis 4:1.

analysis.evidence: Eve remains the subject after וַתֵּלֶד “and she gave birth.” Her first-person verb קָנִיתִי “I have acquired” begins the direct speech introduced by וַתֹּאמֶר.
analysis.morphology: Qal wayyiqtol, third person feminine singular, with prefixed וַ־.

analysis.evidence: After Eve gives birth to Cain (קַיִן), she says קָנִיתִי אִישׁ, ‘I have gained a man.’ The verb takes אִישׁ as its direct object and echoes Cain’s name.
analysis.morphology: Qal perfect, first person common singular, with the ending ־תִי.

analysis.evidence: Eve says קָנִיתִי אִישׁ, “I have acquired a man,” immediately after וַתֵּלֶד אֶת קַיִן, “she gave birth to Cain.” The noun refers to her newborn son.
analysis.morphology: Common noun, masculine singular absolute, without prefix or suffix.

analysis.evidence: In קָנִיתִי אִישׁ, “I have acquired a man,” אִישׁ is the direct object. The following phrase אֶת יַהְוֶה names Yahweh as the one with whose help Eve says she acquired the child.
analysis.morphology: אֶת is the short form of the preposition אֵת. It has no prefix or pronominal suffix.

analysis.evidence: Eve names Yahweh at the end of her statement קָנִיתִי אִישׁ אֶת יַהְוֶה. The preceding אֶת is a separate word, and its interpretation leaves the identity of the divine name clear.
analysis.morphology: Hebrew proper noun in the absolute state, with no prefix or suffix.
analysis.sense: Personal name of the God of Israel
